en: The Thirteen-Book Collection of Birth Stories (Jātaka),
Chapter on Mangoes (Ambavagga)
9. The Rurumiga-rāja Jātaka:
“I give him that excellent village, and women adorned with ornaments.”
“He who describes this deer to me,
the supreme among deer”—
“Give me a choice village.”
And women adorned with ornaments;
I shall give you a deer,
the most excellent of deer.
In this forest grove,
mangoes and sal trees are in bloom,
covered with indragopaka insects.
"Right here this deer stands.
Having made his bow unbending,
he fixed an arrow and approached.
And seeing the king from afar, the deer addressed him:
"Come hither, Great King."
"Do not strike me, O bull among charioteers!
Who has told you this—
that a deer stands right here?"
“That man of evil conduct stands far away from you, O Righteous One;
he has told this to me.”
"Right here this deer stands.
"Truly, it seems, as some men here have said," [he replied].
"A piece of wood that has washed ashore is better than even a single man.
"Ruru, why do you reproach the deer?"
What fear do birds have, or what fear indeed do humans have,
that such an unprecedented terror has seized me upon hearing that human woman speaking?
“When I was rescuing what was being carried away by the vehicle in the great waters,
the flood with its swift current;
because of that, fear came upon me.”
"Indeed, O King, association with the wicked is suffering.
"I shall release this fourfold-winged bird,
which pierces the body, into my heart;"
"I blame that betrayer of friends who does what ought not to be done,
he who does not recognize such a deed as it has been performed.
"O Lord of Men, between the wise man and the fool..."
The virtuous never praise killing;
let the one of evil nature go home as he wishes,
but give him whatever he has lost.
"And I shall be at your service.
"Truly, Ruru, he is one among the virtuous who does not betray a human being after having been betrayed."
"Let that man of evil character go home as he pleases;
whatever was lost by him, that I give to him,
and I grant you freedom to act as you wish."
“The cries of jackals and the calls of birds, O King, as well as the speech of humans, are easy to understand; but the cry of the gods, O King, is difficult to discern.”
It is even more difficult to recognize than that:
even if a person thinks,
"He is my relative," or "He is my friend," or "He is my companion."
“He who was cheerful before,
but afterwards becomes otherwise.
“The people of the countryside have assembled;”
The guilds have assembled together;
deer are devouring the crops—
may Your Majesty restrain them.”
“Let the countryside perish, and let the kingdom as well;
I would never deceive Ruru.”
Having given the gift of fearlessness:
"Let my province not exist,
and let even my kingdom perish."
"But having given a boon to the king of deer, I would never speak a falsehood.
Thus ends the ninth Jātaka, the Ruru Deer King Jātaka.
